Cluster bombs are usually air-dropped shells that eject multiple small bomblets to kill enemy soldiers. The countries also agreed never to develop, acquire, retain or transfer cluster munitions. Countries attending the 11-day conference agreed to the treaty Wednesday but formally signed it Friday. The accord calls for a total, immediate ban of the weapons, strong standards to protect those injured by them, contaminated areas to be cleaned up as quickly as possible and for the weapons to be immediately destroyed, he said. Thomas Nash, coordinator of the CMC campaigning organization, said Wednesday: "This is a great achievement for everyone who has been working hard to see the end of 40 years of suffering from these weapons." Though some of the biggest makers of cluster bombs, including the United States, Russia, China and Israel, were not involved in the talks and have not signed the accord, organizers predicted that those nations would nevertheless be pressured into compliance. "Take the United States," Nash said. "Almost all of its allies are here. They've decided to ban these weapons. That's going to make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the United States to ever use these weapons again, either on its own or in joint operations." The agreement requires the destruction of stockpiles of the weapons within eight years, he said. That means unexploded bomblets lie scattered across a target area, often exploding only when handled or disturbed -- posing a serious risk to civilians. Last week, Acting Assistant Secretary for Political-Military Affairs Stephen D. Mull called it "an absolute moral obligation" to rid a battlefield of unexploded ordnance after the battle. But he also predicted that the United States would not agree to any ban. "We think that it is going to be impossible to ban cluster munitions... because these are weapons that have a certain military utility and are of use," Mull said. "The United States relies on them as an important part of our own defense strategy." Instead, he urged that the weapons be regulated "to take humanitarian considerations into account" and that "technological fixes" be pursued that would render them harmless after a battle. During the 34-day war in Lebanon in 2006, the United Nations estimated that Israel dropped 4 million bomblets, 1 million of which may not have exploded, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross. More than 250 civilians and bomb-disposal operators have been killed or injured by them in southern Lebanon since the war ended. Cluster bombs were also used in the 1999 war in Kosovo. Lt. Col. Jim Burke, a military adviser to the Irish Defense Forces said they quickly became a major killer of civilians. In more than 20 countries, according to the ICRC, cluster bombs have created lasting "no-go" areas, rendering them as dangerous as minefields. Laos is the most affected country. Millions of bomblets dropped during the Vietnam War continue to kill civilians more than three decades later. Still, militaries consider cluster bombs important for use against multiple targets dispersed over a wide area, such as tanks or military personnel moving across the landscape. A single bomb containing hundreds of submunitions can cover more than 18 square miles. CNN's Jacqueline Clyne contributed to this report.

Cluster bombs are typically air-dropped shells that release multiple small bomblets intended to kill enemy soldiers. They also agreed never to develop, acquire, retain or transfer cluster munitions.

Delegates at the 11-day conference agreed to the treaty Wednesday and formally signed it Friday. The accord calls for a total and immediate ban on the weapons, strong standards to protect those injured by them, the swift clearance of contaminated areas, and the immediate destruction of the weapons, he said.

Although some of the largest producers of cluster bombs—including the United States, Russia, China and Israel—were not involved in the talks and have not signed the accord, organizers predicted those nations would nevertheless face pressure to comply.

“Take the United States,” Nash said. “Almost all of its allies are here. They’ve decided to ban these weapons. That’s going to make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the United States to ever use these weapons again, either on its own or in joint operations.”

The agreement requires the destruction of stockpiles of the weapons within eight years, he said.

Cluster munitions, which break apart in flight and scatter hundreds of smaller bomblets, are what the International Committee of the Red Cross calls a “persistent humanitarian problem.” Most of a cluster bomb’s bomblets are designed to explode on impact, but many fail to do so. Estimates indicate that the weapons fail to explode on impact between 10 and 40 percent of the time, the Red Cross says.

As a result, unexploded bomblets remain scattered across a target area, often detonating only when handled or disturbed—posing a serious risk to civilians.

Last week, Acting Assistant Secretary for Political-Military Affairs Stephen D. Mull called it “an absolute moral obligation” to clear a battlefield of unexploded ordnance after combat has ended. But he also predicted that the United States would not agree to any ban.

“We think that it is going to be impossible to ban cluster munitions... because these are weapons that have a certain military utility and are of use,” Mull said. “The United States relies on them as an important part of our own defense strategy.”

Instead, he urged that the weapons be regulated “to take humanitarian considerations into account” and that “technological fixes” be pursued to render them harmless after a battle.

During the 34-day war in Lebanon in 2006, the United Nations estimated that Israel dropped 4 million bomblets, 1 million of which may not have exploded, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross. More than 250 civilians and bomb-disposal operators have been killed or injured by them in southern Lebanon since the war ended.

Cluster bombs were also used in the 1999 war in Kosovo. Lt. Col. Jim Burke, a military adviser to the Irish Defense Forces, said they quickly became a major killer of civilians.

According to the ICRC, cluster bombs have created lasting “no-go” areas in more than 20 countries, making them as dangerous as minefields. Laos is the most affected country. Millions of bomblets dropped during the Vietnam War continue to kill civilians more than three decades later.

Still, militaries consider cluster bombs important for use against multiple targets dispersed over a wide area, such as tanks or military personnel moving across the landscape. A single bomb containing hundreds of submunitions can cover more than 18 square miles.

**More than 100 countries adopt treaty banning cluster bombs**

**DUBLIN, Ireland** — More than 100 countries agreed Wednesday to a landmark treaty banning cluster bombs, weapons that humanitarian groups say have killed and maimed civilians long after conflicts have ended.

The agreement, adopted at a diplomatic conference in Dublin, prohibits the use, production, transfer and stockpiling of cluster munitions. It also requires countries to destroy existing stockpiles, clear contaminated areas and provide assistance to victims.

Cluster bombs are weapons that open in midair and scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller explosives, known as bomblets, over a wide area. While designed to attack enemy troops, vehicles or runways, they are controversial because they can blanket populated areas and because many bomblets fail to explode on impact. Those unexploded submunitions can remain deadly for years, posing risks to farmers, children and returning civilians.

Humanitarian organizations hailed the agreement as a major step in protecting civilians from weapons they say are inherently indiscriminate.

“This treaty will save lives,” campaigners said, arguing that the ban stigmatizes cluster munitions in the same way the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty helped reduce the use of anti-personnel land mines.

The push for a ban gained momentum after conflicts in places such as Lebanon, Laos, Kosovo, Iraq and Afghanistan, where unexploded bomblets left behind dangerous contamination. In southern Lebanon, large numbers of cluster munitions were fired during the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah, prompting renewed international pressure for restrictions.

But several major military powers did not join the treaty, including the United States, Russia, China and Israel. Those countries have argued that cluster munitions can have legitimate military uses when employed under strict rules, and they have resisted a total ban.

The absence of those nations means the treaty will not immediately eliminate the weapons from the arsenals of some of the world’s largest militaries. Still, supporters say the agreement creates a powerful international norm that could make future use of cluster bombs increasingly unacceptable.

The treaty is expected to be formally signed later this year in Oslo, Norway, and will enter into force after a required number of countries ratify it.

**Nations Agree in Dublin to Ban Cluster Munitions**

**DUBLIN, May 30, 2008** — More than 100 nations agreed Friday on a landmark treaty banning the use, production, transfer and stockpiling of cluster munitions, weapons blamed for killing and maiming civilians long after conflicts end.

The agreement, reached at a diplomatic conference in Dublin, marked a major victory for humanitarian campaigners who have argued that cluster bombs pose an unacceptable risk to civilians. The weapons scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller bomblets over wide areas, and many fail to explode on impact, leaving behind deadly hazards similar to land mines.

Thomas Nash, coordinator of the Cluster Munition Coalition, hailed the agreement as a historic achievement, calling it “a major victory” for civilians affected by war. Campaigners said the treaty would stigmatize the weapons even among countries that do not immediately join.

Under the convention, signatory states would be required to destroy stockpiles within eight years, clear contaminated areas within 10 years and provide assistance to victims and affected communities. The treaty also includes provisions aimed at helping survivors receive medical care, rehabilitation and social support.

The United States, Russia, China, Israel, India and Pakistan did not participate in the Dublin negotiations and are not expected to join the treaty in the near term. Washington has maintained that cluster munitions remain militarily useful when used under strict controls.

Stephen Mull, a senior U.S. State Department official, said the United States shared concerns about civilian casualties but could not support a blanket ban. He argued that cluster munitions have “military utility” and said U.S. policy focused on improving reliability and reducing unexploded ordnance rather than prohibiting the weapons altogether.

Supporters of the treaty said the absence of major military powers would not undermine the agreement’s impact. They pointed to the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty, which helped create a strong international norm against antipersonnel land mines despite the refusal of some major powers to join.

The Dublin agreement came after years of pressure from governments, aid groups and survivors, particularly following conflicts in Lebanon, Kosovo, Iraq and Afghanistan, where unexploded submunitions caused civilian casualties after fighting ended.

The convention was scheduled to be formally signed in Oslo later in 2008. Humanitarian groups said the Dublin outcome represented one of the most significant advances in disarmament since the land mine ban.

**Nations sign treaty banning cluster bombs; U.S. declines to join**

*OSLO, Norway —* More than 100 countries have endorsed a new international treaty banning the use, production, transfer and stockpiling of cluster munitions, weapons that human-rights groups say pose a long-term threat to civilians long after wars end.

The agreement, known as the Convention on Cluster Munitions, requires participating nations to destroy their stockpiles within eight years, clear contaminated areas within 10 years and provide assistance to victims. It also prohibits countries from helping others use or transfer the weapons.

Cluster bombs are typically dropped from aircraft or fired by artillery, rockets or missiles. They open in midair and scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller explosive submunitions over a wide area. Military planners have used them to attack concentrations of troops, armored vehicles, airfields and other broad targets.

But the weapons have drawn intense criticism because they cannot distinguish between soldiers and civilians when used near populated areas. In addition, many submunitions fail to explode on impact. Those unexploded bomblets can remain lethal for years, effectively becoming land mine-like hazards that kill or injure civilians, including children who may pick them up.

The International Committee of the Red Cross, the United Nations and disarmament groups have cited civilian casualties in conflicts in Southeast Asia, the Balkans, Iraq, Afghanistan and Lebanon. In southern Lebanon, large numbers of unexploded submunitions were left after the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah, according to U.N. and aid agencies.

Supporters of the treaty say it establishes a new global norm against a weapon they consider inherently indiscriminate in populated areas.

“This is a major step for the protection of civilians,” said advocates involved in the negotiations, who argued that the humanitarian cost of cluster munitions outweighs their military value.

Several major military powers, however, did not join the treaty, including the United States, Russia and China. Israel, India and Pakistan also remained outside the agreement.

The United States said it would not sign because cluster munitions remain part of its defense strategy and could be needed in certain battlefield situations, particularly where large-area effects are required. U.S. officials have argued that a complete ban could endanger American troops and allies.

At the same time, Washington has said it supports reducing harm to civilians. The U.S. has pursued policies aimed at limiting the use of older, less reliable cluster munitions and improving the reliability of submunitions so fewer fail to detonate. Critics say such measures do not go far enough and that even low failure rates can leave large numbers of unexploded explosives when weapons are used at scale.

The treaty emerged through a diplomatic process launched in Oslo after efforts within traditional arms-control forums stalled. Its backers include many European, African and Latin American countries, as well as nations affected by unexploded cluster munitions.

The agreement will enter into force after a required number of countries ratify it. Once binding, states that are party to the treaty will be required to halt use of the weapons and begin clearance and destruction programs.

Advocates say the treaty could influence even countries that do not sign, by stigmatizing the weapons and discouraging their use. Opponents of a total ban say any restrictions should balance humanitarian concerns with military needs.

For civilians living in former battle zones, the practical impact will depend on how quickly contaminated land is cleared and whether non-signatory countries continue to use or supply the weapons in future conflicts.

### Nations formally adopt cluster bomb ban treaty in Ireland

Diplomats from more than 100 countries formally adopted a landmark treaty in Dublin, Ireland, banning the use, production, transfer and stockpiling of cluster munitions, weapons blamed for killing and maiming civilians long after wars have ended.

The agreement, reached after nearly two weeks of negotiations, was hailed by disarmament advocates as a major humanitarian breakthrough. The Cluster Munition Coalition, or CMC, an international network of non-governmental organizations campaigning against the weapons, called the adoption of the treaty a historic step toward protecting civilians from weapons that have caused widespread harm in conflicts around the world.

Cluster bombs are typically dropped from aircraft or fired by artillery and rockets. They open in midair and scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller explosive submunitions over a broad area. Many explode on impact, but a significant number fail to detonate immediately, effectively becoming land mines that can kill or injure civilians years later.

The International Committee of the Red Cross has estimated that cluster munitions often leave behind large numbers of unexploded bomblets, with failure rates that can vary widely depending on the weapon and conditions. Humanitarian groups say the danger is especially severe because the small bomblets can be mistaken by children for toys or scrap metal.

The treaty adopted in Dublin requires participating nations to destroy their stockpiles of cluster munitions within eight years. It also obliges countries to clear contaminated areas, assist victims and provide support to affected communities. The agreement bans the use, production and transfer of the weapons, although negotiators debated exceptions for newer weapons designed to reduce unexploded remnants.

Campaigners pointed to recent and historic conflicts as evidence of the need for a ban. In Lebanon, cluster munitions were used extensively during the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah. Large numbers of unexploded submunitions remained after the fighting ended, posing a continuing threat to civilians returning to their homes and farms.

Cluster bombs were also used during NATO’s 1999 air campaign in Kosovo, where unexploded submunitions caused civilian casualties after the conflict. Laos remains one of the most heavily contaminated countries in the world because of cluster munitions dropped during the Vietnam War era; decades later, civilians there are still killed or injured by unexploded ordnance.

Supporters of the ban compared the Dublin agreement to the 1997 treaty prohibiting anti-personnel land mines, saying it reflected growing international acceptance that weapons with indiscriminate and long-lasting effects should be outlawed.

However, several major military powers were not part of the negotiations or did not support the treaty, including the United States, Russia and China. Other countries with significant stockpiles or histories of cluster munition use also stayed outside the process, raising questions about how quickly the norm against the weapons would spread.

Despite those absences, campaigners and supportive governments said the treaty would stigmatize cluster munitions and make their future use politically costly, even for countries that do not immediately join.

The treaty was scheduled to be opened for signature later in Oslo, Norway. Once ratified by enough countries, it would enter into force and create binding obligations for states that join.

(CNN) -- More than 100 countries attending a conference in Dublin, Ireland, have agreed on the text of a landmark treaty that would ban the use, production, transfer and stockpiling of cluster munitions, weapons that campaigners say have killed and maimed thousands of civilians long after wars have ended.

The accord, reached after intensive negotiations, is being hailed by disarmament advocates as one of the most significant humanitarian arms-control agreements in a decade. It would prohibit a broad category of cluster bombs, rockets and artillery shells that scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller explosive submunitions over wide areas.

Supporters say the ban is necessary because the weapons are inherently indiscriminate when used near populated areas and because many of their bomblets fail to explode on impact, remaining lethal for years as de facto land mines. Children are frequently among the victims, drawn to the small, brightly colored devices.

“This treaty is about protecting civilians during war and after war,” said one campaign representative involved in the talks. “Cluster munitions have left a deadly legacy in country after country. The world is saying that legacy must end.”

But the agreement has also exposed a deep divide between governments and militaries that view the weapons as outdated and unacceptable, and those that argue they still serve a legitimate battlefield purpose when used under strict rules.

Several major military powers — including the United States, Russia and China — did not participate in the Dublin negotiations and are not expected to join the treaty in the near term. Their absence means that while the accord carries significant moral and diplomatic weight, it will not immediately bind some of the world’s largest producers and users of cluster munitions.

Military officials in countries that have defended retaining the weapons say cluster munitions can be effective against massed armor, airfields, artillery positions and dispersed enemy forces. They argue that modern versions, equipped with self-destruct or self-deactivation mechanisms, can reduce the danger to civilians compared with older designs.

Critics counter that technical fixes have not eliminated the problem of unexploded ordnance and that the area effect of the weapons makes them too dangerous in contemporary conflicts, where combat often occurs in or near towns and villages.

The Dublin agreement follows years of campaigning by humanitarian groups and affected communities in places such as Laos, Lebanon, Cambodia, Afghanistan, Iraq and the Balkans. In some of those countries, unexploded cluster submunitions have continued to kill civilians decades after being dropped.

Laos remains one of the starkest examples. During the Vietnam War era, millions of tons of ordnance were dropped over the country, including vast numbers of cluster bomblets. Clearance teams are still finding unexploded submunitions in fields, forests and villages, hampering agriculture and development.

More recently, the use of cluster munitions in the 2006 conflict between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon intensified international pressure for a ban. U.N. officials and rights groups said large numbers of unexploded bomblets were left behind in southern Lebanon, posing a severe hazard to returning civilians.

The treaty text agreed in Dublin requires countries that join to destroy stockpiles within a set period, clear contaminated areas, and provide assistance to victims and affected communities. It also includes provisions intended to promote international cooperation and support for clearance operations.

One of the most contentious issues during negotiations was how to define which weapons would be banned. Some governments sought exemptions for newer munitions designed to meet reliability standards or to target individual objects rather than saturate broad areas. The final text excludes certain weapons with a limited number of submunitions and safeguards intended to minimize unexploded remnants, but campaigners said the treaty still represents a strong prohibition.

Another difficult question centered on military cooperation between treaty members and non-members. Many U.S. allies wanted to ensure that joining the accord would not prevent them from participating in joint operations with countries that continue to possess cluster munitions. The compromise language has been closely scrutinized by legal experts and activists, some of whom fear it could create loopholes, while governments say it preserves the ability to maintain alliances without undermining the ban.

The agreement is part of what has become known as the Oslo Process, launched after efforts to address cluster munitions through traditional arms-control forums stalled. Like the 1997 treaty banning anti-personnel land mines, the new accord was negotiated outside the consensus-based U.N. disarmament system, allowing like-minded states and civil society groups to move more quickly.

That model has drawn praise from humanitarian organizations, which say it shows that governments can act decisively when civilians face unacceptable harm. But skeptics argue that arms-control agreements are less effective when major possessors remain outside them.

“The challenge now is implementation and universalization,” said a diplomat familiar with the talks. “A treaty can change behavior, create stigma and establish a new norm. But it must be backed by real destruction of stockpiles, clearance of contaminated land and pressure on states that remain outside.”

For countries that sign and ratify the agreement, the military implications could be significant. Armed forces may need to revise doctrine, destroy existing arsenals and procure alternative weapons. Some governments have already stopped using cluster munitions or begun phasing them out, while others will face greater costs and logistical challenges.

The debate over military utility is unlikely to disappear. Advocates of cluster munitions say commanders may need area weapons in high-intensity conflicts, especially against large formations or mobile targets. They contend that banning an entire class of weapons may shift militaries toward alternatives that are not necessarily less destructive.

Opponents respond that the humanitarian cost outweighs any claimed advantage. They say precision-guided weapons and other alternatives can achieve military objectives without leaving behind thousands of unexploded bomblets. Above all, they argue, the record of civilian casualties has made cluster munitions politically and morally indefensible.

The accord will be opened for signature later this year, with governments expected to gather in Oslo for a formal signing ceremony. It will enter into force after a specified number of countries ratify it.

For survivors, clearance workers and campaigners, the Dublin breakthrough marks a turning point after years of frustration. Yet they acknowledge that the most dangerous work lies ahead — removing existing explosives from contaminated land and persuading more countries to give up the weapons.

“This is not the end of the story,” one activist said. “It is the beginning of a new international standard: that weapons which cannot distinguish between a soldier today and a child tomorrow have no place in modern warfare.”
